title: Taiwan says AI agents helped hack its government in four days
excerpt: Taiwan says it was targeted in July by an AI-driven hacking campaign that used agents like Open Claw to steal passwords and personnel records in about four days.
content_html:
Taiwan says it spent part of last month fending off a hacking campaign that leaned on artificial intelligence to do the heavy lifting.

The island’s Ministry of Digital Affairs, through its National Institute of Cyber Security, disclosed that government agencies were targeted in July, with alerts going out from around 20 July.

What makes the episode notable is not the break-in itself but the method. According to the ministry, the campaign blended old-fashioned manual hacking with the assistance of AI agents, software that can be pointed at a target and left to reason and act largely on its own. One such agent, “Open Claw”, was cited as an example of the agent-assisted approach.

The result was speed. Over roughly four days the attackers extracted “scores of passwords”, stole personnel records from the justice ministry, and probed a nuclear-safety agency for vulnerabilities.

That kind of breadth once demanded a skilled human team working for weeks, which is partly why the question of who is liable when a rogue AI agent hacks a company has stopped being hypothetical.

The targets were government bodies, and the reported activity ranged from credential theft to broader data extraction. The ministry said the affected units had “successively completed their handling”, and insisted that “the relevant attack sources, methods, and scope of impact have all been fully investigated”.

Officials described the source as overseas but stopped short of naming a culprit, and no threat-actor group has been identified.

The disclosure nonetheless lands amid the persistent tensions between Taiwan and China, and it is not hard to read a subtext into the timing, even if the evidence made public does not spell one out.

The wider context arrived from outside Taiwan. The disclosure follows a report by the cybersecurity firm Dream describing an AI-driven campaign against an unnamed Asian government, later identified as Taiwan by the Financial Times.

That is roughly the sequence in which these stories now tend to surface: a private firm spots the pattern, and the government confirms it afterwards.

For all the talk of autonomous machines, the humans have not left the building. “There’s still a human in there somewhere,” one security researcher cautioned of the campaign. “It’s not totally 100% autonomous.”

The distinction matters, because the AI here is an accelerant rather than a replacement, and accelerants are the sort of thing defenders lose sleep over.

What that acceleration lowers is the barrier to entry. An AI agent recently faked identities to plant malware, and the tools involved are cheap, widely available, and improving fast, which quietly hands the resources of a state to almost anyone willing to run them.

The vulnerabilities cut both ways, mind. Researchers have shown that these agents can be turned against their own operators, in one case tricking an OpenClaw agent into leaking AWS keys and customer data with nothing more than a phishing email. An attacker’s clever assistant is also a fresh attack surface.

Taiwan is, in many respects, the obvious place to watch this play out first. It sits at the sharp end of geopolitical pressure, runs a dense and heavily digitised public sector, and has long served as a proving ground for cyber-techniques that later surface elsewhere.

The compression of time is the part worth dwelling on. What used to be measured in the weeks a human crew needed to move laterally through a network can now, on this evidence, be squeezed into a long weekend, which rewrites the arithmetic for everyone tasked with defending one.

Taiwan says it has since tightened monitoring and issued protective guidance across its agencies. Whether that proves enough is another matter, because if a handful of AI agents can rifle through government systems in four days, the next campaign is unlikely to wait politely for the defenders to catch up.

content_html_zh:
台湾表示，上个月，它花了部分时间来抵御一场依靠人工智能来完成繁重工作的黑客活动。

该岛数字事务部通过国家网络安全研究所透露，政府机构于 7 月成为攻击目标，并于 7 月 20 日左右发出警报。

这一集引人注目的不是闯入行为本身，而是闯入行为的方法。 据该部称，该活动将老式的手动黑客攻击与人工智能代理的协助相结合，人工智能代理是可以指向目标并在很大程度上自行推理和行动的软件。 其中一个代理“Open Claw”被引用为代理辅助方法的一个例子。

结果就是速度。 在大约四天的时间里，攻击者提取了“大量密码”，窃取了司法部的人事记录，并调查了一个核安全机构的漏洞。

这种广度曾经需要一个熟练的人类团队工作数周，这就是为什么当流氓人工智能代理攻击一家公司时谁应该承担责任的问题不再是假设性的。

目标是政府机构，报告的活动范围从凭证盗窃到更广泛的数据提取。 国防部表示，受影响单位已“陆续完成处置”，并坚称“相关攻击来源、方式、影响范围均已全面调查”。

官员称消息来源为海外，但没有指出罪魁祸首，也没有确定任何威胁组织。

尽管如此，这一披露仍然是在台湾和中国大陆之间持续紧张的背景下进行的，而且不难从这个时机中解读出潜台词，即使公开的证据并没有阐明这一点。

更广泛的背景来自台湾以外。 在此披露之前，网络安全公司 Dream 发布了一份报告，描述了一场由人工智能驱动的针对一个未透露姓名的亚洲政府的活动，该政府后来被英国《金融时报》认定为台湾。

现在这些故事的出现大致是这样的顺序：一家私营公司发现了这种模式，然后政府确认了这一点。

尽管人们都在谈论自主机器，但人类并没有离开这座大楼。 “那里的某个地方仍然有人，”一位安全研究人员就此次活动发出警告。 “它并不是完全 100% 自主的。”

这种区别很重要，因为这里的人工智能是一种促进剂，而不是替代品，而促进剂是让防守者失眠的东西。

这种加速降低的是进入壁垒。 一个人工智能代理最近伪造了身份来植入恶意软件，所涉及的工具价格便宜、广泛使用且改进迅速，它悄悄地将一个国家的资源交给了几乎任何愿意运行它们的人。

请注意，这些漏洞是双向的。 研究人员表明，这些代理可以针对自己的运营商，在一种情况下，只需一封网络钓鱼电子邮件即可诱骗 OpenClaw 代理泄露 AWS 密钥和客户数据。 攻击者的聪明助手也是一个新的攻击面。

从很多方面来看，台湾显然是最先观看这场比赛的地方。 它处于地缘政治压力的最前沿，运营着密集且高度数字化的公共部门，并且长期以来一直充当后来在其他地方出现的网络技术的试验场。

时间的压缩是值得深入探讨的部分。 根据这一证据，过去需要用几周的时间来衡量人类人员在网络中横向移动的时间，现在可以压缩到一个长周末，这为每个负责保卫的人重写了算术。

台湾表示，此后加强了监控，并在各机构发布了保护指南。 这是否证明足够是另一回事，因为如果少数人工智能特工可以在四天内席卷政府系统，那么下一场战役就不太可能礼貌地等待防御者赶上。
